definition: Lasting much longer than expected or than usual, often in a tiresome way.
example: After a protracted search, the family finally found an apartment near the park.
nuance: Protracted suggests unwelcome length; prolonged is more neutral and can describe pleasant things, as in prolonged applause.
prompt: A neighborhood committee spends months arguing about where to build a new playground.
options: The protracted debate over the site dragged on through three seasons of meetings.
The protracted debate ended in five minutes when everyone chose the first site.
The protracted committee members pushed back their chairs and refused to vote.
The protracted slide on the new playground stuck out over the sidewalk.
reasons: An argument stretching across many months is exactly the kind of tiresome length the word implies.
A discussion settled in minutes is short, the reverse of something drawn out.
The word describes events or processes that drag on, not people who pull away.
This confuses the word with protruding; sticking out in space is not lasting long in time.

practice.prompt: A mountain town waits for spring after an unusually cold year.
options: The protracted ski lodge stood on the highest ridge above the town.
A protracted winter kept snow on the hiking trails well into May.
The protracted winter ended abruptly after a single mild week in January.
The protracted puddle shrank into a tiny circle of ice overnight.
reasons: Being located high up says nothing about something dragging on in time.
Snow lingering months past its usual season shows a cold spell lasting far longer than normal.
A season that quits early is cut short, not stretched out.
Shrinking in size is contraction; the word concerns how long something lasts.
